_comment: Single source for the simulator. cards: store messages; actions: calls your code makes; scenarios: ordered steps (send a card, do an action, toggle database/Play API/acknowledger, register a token Google already knows). Each step that has an outcome carries an expect block written by the Go test (go test -run TestSiteScenarios -update-site .) and checked by it and by site/check-scenarios.js.

scenarios.name: Normal life
scenarios.note: Subscribe, renew, renew. Each message moves the version up by one.

scenarios.name: The store sends it twice
scenarios.note: The second DID_RENEW has the same notification ID, so nothing changes.

scenarios.name: Messages out of order
scenarios.note: The March renewal arrives before the February one. February is older than what is stored.

scenarios.name: Refund, then a bookkeeping message
scenarios.note: After a refund, switching auto-renew off must not give access back. Only a reversal does.

scenarios.name: A forged refund
scenarios.note: The forged message is rejected before it is even read. The user keeps access.

scenarios.name: Refund of an old renewal
scenarios.note: Refunding the February renewal does not end a chain that already runs to April. The refund is recorded against that one transaction.

scenarios.name: A refund before the renewal it does not concern
scenarios.note: February is refunded first, which ends the chain. The March renewal then arrives, signed earlier than the refund, and brings it back because it is a different transaction.

scenarios.name: Google upgrade, then a late message
scenarios.note: Token B closes token A. A late token A event is stale.

scenarios.name: The database blips
scenarios.note: While the database is down the answer is 500 and nothing is recorded, so the retry works.

scenarios.name: A renewal naming another account
scenarios.note: A chain keeps its first owner. A later message that names a different user still moves the state forward, but the owner does not change.

scenarios.name: Link a purchase to a user
scenarios.note: The renewal has no account token, so it is stored without a user and nobody has access. Linking attaches the user. A second link is a no-op, and a different user is refused.

scenarios.name: Find the user when a message arrives
scenarios.note: With a user resolver, your own transaction-to-user table is asked for every message without a user. Here it knows the chain.

scenarios.name: Add-ons: one purchase, two products
scenarios.note: Each line item is stored as its own entitlement, so access is decided per product.

scenarios.name: Google acknowledgement
scenarios.note: The purchase is acknowledged only after it is stored. If Google refuses, the push is retried, the duplicate is skipped, and the acknowledgement is sent again.

scenarios.name: A lost upgrade message
scenarios.note: Only the message for token C arrived. The library asks Google about token B and follows its link to token A, so all three chains end up consistent.

scenarios.name: Repair a lost webhook with Reconcile
scenarios.note: The renewal webhook never arrived. Reconcile asks Apple for the current status and applies it. Running it again changes nothing.

scenarios.name: Refund requests need consent
scenarios.note: Apple asks how much of a purchase was used. The answer is sent only if the customer agreed. If your lookup fails inside 12 hours the answer is 500, so Apple asks again.

scenarios.name: Auto-renew switched off
scenarios.note: The renewal setting is stored next to the state. An active chain with auto-renew off is a churn signal.

scenarios.name: Erase a user
scenarios.note: Erasing deletes the user's entitlements. Event IDs are kept, so a redelivered webhook cannot bring them back.
